qa.q: Why does skipping the vaccine feel safer to Aditi?
qa.a: A rare reaction would feel like the result of Aditi's own choice, while catching the illness would just be bad luck, so doing nothing seems less blameworthy even though the illness is going around.

qa.q: What sensible step does Ishita suggest?
qa.a: Asking the clinic doctor, who knows Aditi's history, about the reaction, and walking there together so the fear gets a real answer.

qa.q: How does Ishita see the choice differently from Aditi?

grounding: It shows a young adult avoiding a recommended vaccine because a rare reaction from acting feels more blameworthy than the larger risk of not acting.

passage:
Sudha didi, the ASHA worker, came down the lane in Rampur with her register. "Mohit, the vaccine camp is at the school tomorrow. You're on my list."
Mohit was fixing the tractor's chain. "I'll see, didi."
"You said that last month."
He wiped his hands on a rag. His cousin in the next village had been feverish for days after a shot once, and people still talked about it at the tea shop. If Mohit took the shot and fell ill, everyone would say he had walked into it himself. If he caught the disease the camp was meant to stop, well, that would be fate.
"This illness has hit three houses in the block this season," Sudha said. "At least come and ask the doctor your doubts."
Mohit nodded without looking up and went back to the chain.

qa.q: Where is the vaccine camp being held?
qa.a: The vaccine camp is at the school tomorrow.

qa.q: Why does falling ill from the disease feel less frightening to Mohit than a reaction to the shot?
qa.a: If he took the shot and got sick, people would say he walked into it himself, but catching the disease would just be fate, so doing nothing feels less blameworthy to him.

qa.q: What could help Mohit weigh the choice more fairly?
qa.a: Going to the camp to ask the doctor his doubts, as Sudha suggests, and setting the three sick houses nearby against one story repeated at the tea shop.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Mohit goes back to the chain without looking up?
qa.a: She may feel frustrated and worried, since she has seen the illness reach three houses and knows he has put this off before.

grounding: It shows a young man delaying a recommended vaccine because harm from acting feels more blameworthy than the larger risk of the disease.

passage:
Wanjiru had kept the email from the university clinic open for three weeks: second dose of the vaccine due, walk-ins on Tuesdays. She kept closing it.
"You going today?" Mina asked, lacing her trainers in their hostel room in Nairobi.
"Maybe next week."
The truth was a forum post she had read at 2 a.m., about a girl who had a rare reaction and felt unwell for weeks. Wanjiru knew it was one story out of thousands. But if she caused something like that by walking into the clinic, she would never forgive herself. If she caught the illness in the lecture halls, at least she hadn't done anything.
Mina paused at the door. "Half our class had it last term, you know."
"I know," Wanjiru said, and pulled the blanket up to her chin.

qa.q: When are walk-ins at the university clinic?
qa.a: Walk-ins are on Tuesdays.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru worried about each time she closed the email?
qa.a: She worried that if the shot caused a rare reaction it would be her own doing and she would never forgive herself, while catching the illness would feel like something that just happened to her.

qa.q: What would you advise Wanjiru to do with her fear?
qa.a: Take the forum post to a clinic nurse or doctor and ask about it directly 🤔, and compare it honestly with how many classmates actually got ill last term.

qa.q: How does Mina see the risk?
qa.a: Mina sees the illness as the common, nearby danger, since half their class had it last term, so Wanjiru's delay probably worries Mina.

grounding: It shows a young adult postponing a vaccine dose because a rare side effect she might cause feels worse than the more common illness.

passage:
The hostel health centre smelled of antiseptic. Kamal sat holding a freshly bandaged palm, cut on the rusty gate of the cycle stand. Rukmini, the nurse, came back with a form. "Doctor says a tetanus shot today."
Kamal stood up. "Actually, I'm fine. I read online about someone who had a bad reaction to it."
"That can happen, very rarely," Rukmini said. "Tetanus itself is far more dangerous."
"But if the shot hurts me, that's because I chose it. If I skip it and get sick, that's just bad luck." He was already at the door.
Rukmini didn't argue. "Then sit with the doctor for five minutes and say exactly what worries you. Your choice after that."
Kamal hesitated, looked at his palm, and sat back down.

qa.q: How did Kamal cut his palm?
qa.a: On the rusty gate of the cycle stand.

qa.q: Why does skipping the shot feel less blameworthy to Kamal?
qa.a: If the shot hurt him it would feel like his own fault, while getting sick after skipping would feel like bad luck, so doing nothing seems safer even though the disease is the bigger danger.

qa.q: What choice did Rukmini offer that helped Kamal reconsider?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, Rukmini suggested five minutes with the doctor to say exactly what worried him, leaving the final choice to him.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel watching Kamal head for the door?
qa.a: Rukmini may feel worried for him, knowing the risk, but also understand his fear and try to keep him talking rather than push.

grounding: A student wants to skip a recommended shot because a rare reaction he chose feels worse than a bigger risk that comes by chance.

passage:
Hi Amandeep,
Thanks for the long voice note. I know you think I'm being silly about the vaccine the college recommended before our volunteering trip to the coast. Let me explain properly.
I read one post about someone who got a rare reaction and was in bed for a week. I can't stop picturing it. If that happens to me, I'll know I walked into the clinic and asked for it. If I skip it and catch the disease on the trip, at least that's bad luck, not my doing.
I know, I know. You said the disease is far more common there than the reaction is here. Maybe my brain is doing the maths backwards.
I haven't booked it. But I haven't deleted the clinic's message either.
Chandrika

qa.q: Where is the volunteering trip going?
qa.a: To the coast.

qa.q: Why does skipping the vaccine feel safer to Chandrika?
qa.a: A reaction after choosing the vaccine would feel like Chandrika's own doing, while catching the disease by skipping would feel like bad luck, so inaction feels less blameworthy.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do next with the clinic's message still saved?
qa.a: Chandrika could book a talk with the clinic's doctor and ask directly about the reaction that feels so frightening, so the choice rests on real information rather than one post.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel reading this reply?
qa.a: Amandeep may still feel worried, but also a little hopeful, since Chandrika admits the maths might be backwards and hasn't deleted the message.

grounding: A young adult avoids a recommended vaccine because a rare reaction feels more blameworthy than a larger risk from the disease.
